query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Enhancing the Mo content to a high level (i.e., Mo1) in the CoCrFeNiMox-Ni/MoS2-Ag-Cr2O3 composite will induce FCC lattice distortion and promote the formation of a hard, Mo-rich σ phase that, together with enhanced high‐temperature oxidation and tribochemical reactions, leads to the formation of a dense, continuous oxide/molybdate glaze. This structural change is expected to reduce the coefficient of friction and wear rate over the sliding temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C compared to the baseline Mo0.2 composite.
generation.material_initial_state: Uniformly ball-milled powder mixtures containing 67.5 wt.% CoCrFeNiMox (with x = 0.2 as baseline), 12.5 wt.% Ni-coated MoS2, 15 wt.% Ag, and 5 wt.% Cr2O3 processed by SPS.
generation.intervention: Increase the Mo content from x = 0.2 to x = 1 in the CoCrFeNiMox-Ni/MoS2-Ag-Cr2O3 composite.
generation.conditions: Spark plasma sintering under vacuum at 40 MPa by heating to 1250 °C (150 °C/min), holding for 3 minutes, followed by furnace cooling. Dry sliding tests in air using a 6 mm Si3N4 ball under an 8 N load, 4 mm rotation radius, 0.15 m/s sliding speed, and 270 m sliding distance at temperatures of room temperature, 200, 400, 600, and 800 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: Increased Mo content causes FCC lattice distortion and promotes the formation of a Mo-rich tetragonal σ phase. At high temperatures, oxidation and tribochemical reactions yield a dense glaze comprising silver molybdates and other oxides.
generation.mechanism: Dissolved Mo contributes to solid-solution strengthening and the σ phase acts as a second-phase reinforcement to suppress plastic deformation. At lower temperatures, the combined action of Ni/MoS2 and Ag facilitates the formation of a low-shear lubricating film, while at high temperatures (600–800 °C) the generated oxide/molybdate glaze separates the sliding surfaces and minimizes friction and material removal.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Mo1 composite is expected to exhibit increased hardness and improved wear resistance, with particularly enhanced performance at high temperatures (notably at 800 °C) due to the formation of a coherent glaze. Although the coefficient of friction may not be lowered at every temperature (especially at the intermediate 200–400 °C range), the overall tribological performance (balance of strength and wear resistance) should be superior compared to the Mo0.2 baseline.
generation.baseline: Mo0.2 composite, characterized by a predominantly FCC solid-solution structure with minimal σ phase, displaying a friction coefficient of 0.66 at room temperature (peaking at 0.75 at 200 °C) and dropping to about 0.21 at 800 °C, with wear rates ranging from 13.1 × 10^-6 mm³/N·m at room temperature to 98.1 × 10^-6 mm³/N·m at 400 °C.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable for dry sliding tests in air against a Si3N4 counterface over the temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C, under an 8 N load, a sliding speed of 0.15 m/s, and a sliding distance of 270 m. The processing and testing conditions are fixed as detailed above.
generation.uncertainty: There is some uncertainty regarding the friction behavior at intermediate temperatures (200–400 °C) due to competing effects of thermal softening and wear track roughening, which may not always result in a friction coefficient lower than that of the baseline.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate the Mo1 composite using the same SPS parameters as for the baseline Mo0.2 composite. Perform ball-on-disk sliding tests in air at room temperature, 200, 400, 600, and 800 °C under an 8 N load using a 6 mm Si3N4 counterface. Characterize the phase structure using X-ray diffraction (XRD) and SEM/EDS to confirm lattice distortion and the σ-phase. Measure Vickers hardness and conduct compression tests for mechanical properties. Use a tribometer to record temperature-dependent friction coefficients and profilometry to evaluate wear scar dimensions and wear rates. Use Raman spectroscopy to detect and analyze the oxide/molybdate glaze formed after high-temperature (800 °C) testing.
measurements: XRD peak shifts and σ-phase identification
SEM/EDS for phase distribution and wear-track mapping
Tribometer measurements of temperature-dependent friction coefficients
Profilometry for wear-scar dimensions and wear rate
Raman spectroscopy for identification of the high-temperature glaze
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mo1 composite does not show increased hardness and improved wear resistance, or if the formation of a coherent high-temperature (800 °C) oxide/molybdate glaze is not observed—resulting in friction coefficients and wear rates similar to or worse than those of the Mo0.2 baseline—the hypothesis must be rejected.
